replacement: But this was a mere catchword for the multitude, since the authors of the revolution were in fact to govern. Still, the Assembly and the Council of the Bean went on meeting. They discussed nothing that the conspirators had not approved, and the conspirators supplied the speakers and reviewed in advance what they would say. Fear, and the sight of how many the conspirators were, shut the mouths of everyone else. If anyone did venture to speak against them, he was soon put to death in some convenient way. No one searched for the murderers, and no justice could be had against them even if they were suspected. The people stayed motionless, so thoroughly cowed that men counted themselves lucky to escape violence even when they kept silent. An exaggerated belief in the number of the conspirators also demoralized the people. The size of the city left them helpless, they had no understanding with one another, and they had no means of finding out how many the conspirators really were. For the same reason no one could open his grief to a neighbor and concert measures to defend himself, since he would have had to speak either to a man he did not know, or to a man he knew but did not trust. Indeed the whole popular party approached one another with suspicion, each thinking his neighbor a party to what was going on. The conspirators had in their ranks men whom no one could ever have believed capable of joining an oligarchy, and it was these men who made the many so suspicious. By confirming the commons in their mistrust of one another, they helped to secure impunity for the few.

Agis, however, did not believe the city was tranquil, or that the commons would surrender their ancient liberty in a moment. He thought that the sight of a large Lacedaemonian force would excite them, if they were not already in commotion, of which he was by no means certain. So he gave the envoys of the Four Hundred an answer that offered no hope of an accommodation. He sent for large reinforcements from Peloponnese, and not long afterwards came down to the very walls of Athens with these troops and his garrison from Decelea. He hoped that civil disturbances might help to bring the Athenians to his terms, or that in the confusion to be expected inside and outside the city they might even surrender without a blow. At all events he thought he would succeed in seizing the Long Walls, stripped of their defenders. However, the Athenians watched him come close up without causing the least disturbance within the city. They sent out their cavalry and a number of heavy infantry, light troops, and archers, who shot down some of his soldiers that came too near and took some arms and dead. At last Agis was convinced. He led his army back, stayed with his own troops in their old position at Decelea, and after a few days in Attica sent the reinforcement home. After this the Four Hundred persisted and sent another embassy to Agis, and now they got a better reception. At his suggestion they dispatched envoys to Lacedaemon to negotiate a treaty, being desirous of making peace.
